opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think this is one of the most important questions in AI right now, and it goes right back to what we did with AlphaGo. The famous example is move 37 in the second game against Lee Sedol. That was a move no human professional would have played. The commentators thought it was a mistake at first, and it turned out to be pivotal. The system didn't get that from copying human games. It came from combining a learned model of the game with search, exploring possibilities beyond what was in the training data.

I think the general recipe is this. First, you need a good model of the environment, whether that's the rules of Go, the physics of protein folding, or the dynamics of some scientific domain. That model gives you intuition about which directions are promising. Then you layer search or planning on top of that intuition, so you aren't evaluating every possibility, which would be intractable. Instead you explore the most promising branches more deeply. In Go there are more possible board positions than atoms in the universe, so brute force is hopeless. But a learned value function plus guided search lets you go somewhere genuinely new.

The other key ingredient is an objective function, some way of knowing whether you've found something good. In games that's easy: you win or you lose. In science it's harder, but in some areas you have it. With AlphaFold, for example, there's a measurable notion of how close you are to the real structure. In mathematics you can verify proofs. In code you can run tests. Those domains with clear verification are where I think search-based discovery will flourish first.

Where it gets really interesting is combining that with today's large foundation models. They have an enormous amount of world knowledge, which is a kind of very rich prior. But on their own they mostly interpolate within what they've seen. If you add search, planning, and the ability to test hypotheses, you have something closer to how a scientist works: generate ideas, evaluate them, discard most of them, and refine the good ones.

I like to distinguish three levels of creativity. There's interpolation, which is averaging what you've seen. There's extrapolation, which is something like move 37, new within a domain. Then there's true invention, which would be coming up with Go itself, a new game or a new scientific theory. Current systems can clearly do the first, and with search they can do the second. The third is still an open frontier. Getting there may need more than search, perhaps better ways of choosing what problems are worth posing in the first place. That's one of the things we're most excited to work on.

r001.rationale: It says AlphaGo combined a learned model with search to explore beyond its training data, and recommends adding search to a model to discover new possibilities.

r002.rationale: It explicitly identifies an objective function as necessary for knowing whether a discovery is good, with examples of verification.

r003.rationale: It does not suggest searching the space of programs or that this could generalize to essentially everything.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think about a lot, actually, because I think it's one of the most important questions in the field right now. There's this debate about whether these systems can only ever regurgitate or remix what's in their training data, or whether they can actually come up with something genuinely new. And I think the answer is that search is really the key ingredient.

If you look back at AlphaGo, the famous example is move 37 in the second game against Lee Sedol. That was a move that no human would have played. The system estimated something like a one in ten thousand probability that a human would make that move. And yet it turned out to be a brilliant move, maybe the most beautiful move in the history of the game. Now, where did that come from? It didn't come from imitating human games. It came from the system searching through the space of possibilities, guided by its learned intuition, and discovering something beyond what was in its training distribution.

So the way I think about it is that you have two components. You have the model, which is like intuition, like a very good prior over what's plausible. And then you have the search process, which is like deliberate reasoning. The model narrows down the enormous space of possibilities to something tractable, and the search explores that space, evaluates, and can find things that lie outside of what the model alone would have produced. And crucially, you need some kind of ground truth or objective function to search against. In Go it's winning the game. In mathematics it's whether the proof checks. In protein folding it's whether the structure matches experimental reality. That feedback signal is what lets search push beyond mimicry into genuine discovery.

I actually think about creativity as having levels. The first level is interpolation, where you just produce an average of what you've seen. The second is extrapolation, where you push beyond the known data in a particular direction, and move 37 is an example of that. And then there's the third level, which is what I'd call true invention or out-of-the-box thinking, where you come up with a whole new framework, like Einstein coming up with general relativity. I think current systems are clearly capable of the first level, and with search they're getting to the second. We haven't seen the third yet. I don't think we're far off in principle, but I think it requires something more, maybe the ability to search over the space of hypotheses or questions themselves, not just over answers to a fixed question.

And that's what excites me about the scientific applications. Think about something like AlphaFold, or the work we've done on materials discovery, where the system proposed millions of new stable crystals. Those are domains where there's a huge combinatorial space, far too large for any human to explore exhaustively, but where we can verify whether an answer is right. That's exactly the setting where search-based AI shines. The system can propose, test, and refine at a scale and speed no human laboratory could match, and some fraction of what it finds will be genuinely new to science.

So I'd say, to directly answer your question, search is how you get from a system that knows what we know to a system that can find what we don't know. The model gives you taste. The search gives you discovery. And I think the combination of those two is going to be the engine of scientific progress over the next decade.

r001.rationale: It says search, guided by the model’s learned intuition, can discover possibilities beyond what the model alone would produce.

r002.rationale: It states that search needs a ground truth or objective function to evaluate discoveries, with examples such as winning a game or checking a proof.

r003.rationale: It proposes searching over hypotheses or questions, but does not mention searching programs or suggest that this could generalize to essentially everything.

astra-6.text:
I think search is a very powerful ingredient, because learning from existing data doesn’t have to mean simply reproducing what’s already there. You can learn a model of a domain, and then use that model to explore possibilities that nobody has explicitly shown you.

Take Go. The rules are fixed, but the space of possible games is enormous. You can’t enumerate it. So the interesting question is: can you learn enough about the structure of that space to search the promising parts? And occasionally you find a move that looks strange through the lens of human experience, but turns out to be very effective.

In science, you could imagine doing something similar with a candidate molecule or a mathematical conjecture. The system proposes possibilities, explores their consequences, and uses feedback to refine its search. But there’s a crucial distinction: something being new doesn’t make it useful or true. You need a way to evaluate it. In a game, that’s relatively straightforward. In science, ultimately, you have to connect back to experiment or proof.

So I think a lot of the potential lies in combining a learned understanding of the world with search, and then with rigorous verification. The model gives you an intuition about where to look; search lets you go beyond the examples you’ve seen.

r001.rationale: The response says a learned model can guide search beyond examples already seen, allowing exploration of possibilities not explicitly shown in the data.

r002.rationale: It mentions evaluating discoveries and using feedback to refine search, but does not state that an optimization objective is needed to guide the search.

r003.rationale: The response discusses searching possibilities in Go and science, but does not suggest searching a space of programs or that this approach could generalize to essentially everything.

sol-6.1.text:
I think search is a very powerful ingredient, because it allows a system to go beyond the examples it’s seen and explore the consequences of what it’s learned. You learn a model of the world, and then you ask: what happens if I try this? And what happens if I take that idea another ten steps?

Games make that very clear. The rules are fixed, but the space of possibilities is enormous. You can discover a strategy that nobody has written down or demonstrated, simply by exploring that space intelligently. The learning guides the search, and the search can, in turn, uncover things that improve the learning.

The challenge in science is that we don’t have a perfect simulator or a simple definition of winning. So you need to search over hypotheses, but also work out which experiments would distinguish between them. And ultimately, nature has to tell you whether you’re right. Producing something surprising is one part of discovery; producing something surprising that actually works is the crucial next step.

r001.rationale: The response says search lets a system go beyond examples it has seen by exploring consequences of its learned model.

r002.rationale: It notes that science lacks a simple definition of winning and discusses experiments that distinguish hypotheses, but does not state that an optimization objective is needed to guide the search.

r003.rationale: It discusses exploring possibilities in games and hypotheses in science, but does not suggest that searching programs could generalize to essentially everything.
